newsitem.title: UK: Far East gold demand down through September - CRU.
newsitem.headline: Far East gold demand down through September - CRU.

text.p: Imports by the six major eastern gold destinations were down 16 percent during the first eight months of 1996 compared with the same period last year, according to CRU International's latest Precious Metals Monitor.
Including September, the fall is 15 percent against 1995.
"Moreover, the extent of the decline is being masked by the buoyancy of Indian demand where offtake has remained good for much of the year," the report said.
Imports to most of the other markets in the area have either been stagnant or declining with Japan registering the most acute turndown with a 50 percent fall in imports.
"The main factor behind poor Japanese demand is the weakness of the yen which has pushed the local gold price up by a third in comparison with last year's low," according to the report.
Kilo-bars have traded at a discount to loco London prices in a market with "a natural premium" -- less than a decade ago, premiums reached $2.00-$4.00 per ounce in Tokyo.
Tocom futures volume across the board has been even harder hit. September turnover was 40 percent down on last year with gold business recording a decline of nearly 84 percent.
First nine months bullion imports to Hong Kong were down by about a third, according to CRU's publication.
Subdued demand from China is one influence and reflects the success of the government in reducing inflation to five-six percent in August from 20-25 percent a couple of years ago.
Consequently gold has lost its inflation hedge appeal while the economic austerity programme has crimped consumer spending
"Most important of all the financial liberalisation drive has been sustained, steadily adding potential outlets for private savings," the report said.
Taiwan's imports from Hong Kong have also been down leaving dealers to run off the excess stock built when tensions with China were at their peak in March-April this year.
Trends in South East Asia were more positive. Singapore's first nine months' imports have climbed back to 1995 levels, averaging just under 30 tonnes a month.
But the pattern is uneven with Thailand the strongest market, others steady and Indonesia very quiet.
On the supply side, CRU saw "a modest rally in gold or a slip in the Australian dollar-U.S. dollar rate...certain to trigger a round of sales" from the producers.
This was partly due to a jump in Australian production costs, highlighted by Gold Fields Mineral Services, of $50 to $290 in the second quarter this year.
If the South African rand stabilises after its collapse earlier in the year, pressure to secure operating margins on high-cost South African producers could grow, the report said.
